**Rebuttal for 336**

Debater B's main charge rests on a misreading. Column 4 of my 6×6 table is (3, 1, 9, 45, 5, 15), not (1, 1, 9, 45, 5, 15). Its entries are exactly the divisors of 45: 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 45. I checked all six rows and all six columns against {12, 20, 18, 45, 50, 75}, and each is the full divisor set of its number. The six numbers are distinct. So S(3)=6 is verified, and B's claim that the table "fails" is false.

B also concedes that its own values, S(5)=10, S(7)=14, S(11)=22, and S(13)=26, have no tables. The 80 answer therefore has no construction behind it at any size beyond n=2. Its odd-prime impossibility argument is a sketch that B admits is unproven.

I should be candid about my side's gaps. The m=5, 7, 11, 13 cases of the ordered-pair construction are asserted rather than written out, and the minimality argument for n=10, 14, and so on is only sketched. But the question is which claim has evidence. The 6×6 table is checkable and correct, and the n=p exclusion follows from the fact that numbers with p divisors are prime powers. Until B exhibits a 10×10 divisoral table, 80 is unsupported, and 336 is the better-supported answer.
